sections.html:
The county sits on Ohio's southern edge, across the Ohio River from Kentucky. Deeds are recorded in Georgetown, the seat, at the Administration Building, 800 Mt. Orab Pike, Suite 151, Georgetown, Ohio 45121. Two other offices you will need share the building: the auditor in Suite 181 and the treasurer in Suite 171.

Brown County counted 43,676 residents in 2020 and is estimated at 44,397 for July 2025. Of its 19,965 housing units, 77.2 percent are owner-occupied, and the median owned home is worth $196,200.

Recording charges are fixed by state law. Each is split evenly between a basic fee and a contribution to the Ohio Housing Trust Fund (sections 317.32 and 317.36), and most common documents share a single price.

Brown County Recorder fees for common documents
Document or serviceFee
Deed, mortgage, lease or affidavit, up to two pages$39.00
Each additional page or attachment$8.00
Non-standard document$20.00 per document
Plat, 18 by 24 inches$50.40
Copy, per page$2.00
Certified copy, per page$2.00, plus $1.00 for the seal
UCC financing statement$12.00 plus $4.00 per name indexed

Add $5.00 for a federal tax lien and $3.00 for its release. Recording a living will or health care power of attorney costs $40.00, and a first certified copy of a military discharge is free. A Medicaid estate recovery notice of pending transfer is also linked on the recorder's site.

Make sure the deed carries all nine of these before it goes anywhere:

  • The Tax Map office stamp of approval for the transfer.
  • The auditor's transfer endorsement.
  • The seller's name.
  • The buyer's name and mailing address.
  • The seller's original signature and the date, with the name typed or printed beneath.
  • A notary acknowledgement.
  • A legal description giving the county, the township or village, and the acreage.
  • The parcel identification number.
  • A preparation statement.

The recorder's staff cannot draw up documents, sell forms or give legal advice, so most sellers use a title company or attorney for the draft.

Every transfer needs a conveyance or exemption form, and every deed needs a parcel number. To avoid the non-standard fee, use type of 10 points or more on letter or legal paper in black or blue ink, no highlighting, with 1-inch margins at the sides and bottom and 3 inches clear at the top of page one.

Several kinds of paper reach this counter in a house sale. Deeds come in many forms, among them warranty, survivorship, quit claim and sheriff's deeds, plus certificates of transfer. Mortgages arrive with their releases, assignments, assumptions, subordinations and amendments. Land contracts, affidavits, easements and leases are also recorded, along with plats and condominium drawings, powers of attorney, trusts and bills of sale. Liens fit in too: mechanic's liens, federal tax liens and homeowner association liens, plus notices of commencement.

Military service discharges, zoning resolutions with maps, annexations and street name changes are filed here as well. If something that touches your house is in the public record, from an old mortgage to a lien, it came through this counter. Whoever buys will have a title company read all of it, so an unfiled mortgage release is a loose end worth tying up before you list.

Whether you walk in or mail it, the deed has to clear the auditor and the county's Tax Map department.

  • In person. Begin with the recorder, who checks the document against the office's requirements and fees. Then step over to the auditor's office to complete the conveyance. The Tax Map department then picks up the deed at the Engineer Building in Georgetown.
  • By mail. Mail the deed to the recorder at Suite 151 with a cover note and phone number, a check made out to Brown County Recorder, every auditor fee and form, and a self-addressed stamped envelope.

Tax Map works through documents in the order they arrive, so nobody can hurry a deed through. It checks legal descriptions, so phone the department about its requirements. After Tax Map and the auditor stamp the deed, it goes back to the recorder for recording. The auditor can answer questions at 937-378-6398.

Locally, the auditor charges $4.00 of transfer fee and conveyance tax per $1,000 of purchase price, plus fifty cents for each parcel number. Every transfer also needs a conveyance or exemption form.

Two laws stand behind it. The auditor's statement-of-value fee is covered by section 319.54(G)(3). A county may also levy a deed transfer tax under section 322.02, no higher than 30 cents per $100. The grantor listed on the deed owes it, and it is settled with the auditor before the deed is recorded. Exempt transfers such as family gifts use an exemption statement instead of a value statement.

If you think your transfer is exempt, ask the auditor which box to check before you sign.

Property tax goes to the county treasurer, 937-378-6705, and the counter is open weekdays 8:00 to 4:00. Deadlines are not fixed from year to year. Ohio House Bill 186 created an inflation cap credit on certain school district levies and pushed the latest second-half deadline later, so phone the treasurer for the current schedule.

Owners who fall behind can ask the treasurer for a payment plan, and a monthly escrow program lets owners pay ahead of the bill in smaller pieces. Paying online adds convenience fees, among them $1.50 for an electronic check. The auditor's site lists 35,315 parcels in the county and notes that the homestead exemption is the relief available to seniors, disabled owners and qualifying disabled service members.

Your title company should request the parcel's balance from the treasurer ahead of closing. Cash deals need it as well, though they can wrap up sooner with no lender in the loop.

sections.h2: Why the Tax Map stop matters
sections.html:
Many sellers expect the recorder to be the last word on a deed, but in Brown County the Tax Map department checks the legal description first. If the description is wrong or fails to fit your parcel, the deed stalls there and nothing gets recorded. That is why the recorder suggests calling the department about its requirements before you submit. Because Tax Map takes documents in the order they arrive, a deed submitted the week of closing can sit in line, so build some slack into your timeline.

For a quick sale, the practical step is to get the legal description and parcel number right in the draft, line up the auditor's forms, and submit early. Cash buyers often want a short closing, and the office stamps are the part you cannot rush.

sections.h2: Putting it together as a seller
sections.html:
The right sequence saves trips. A title company or attorney drafts the deed, legal description and parcel number included, and the seller signs before a notary. The recorder checks it and the fee, the auditor endorses it, and Tax Map stamps it. Then it returns to the recorder to go on record. Mailing it in means enclosing every auditor fee and form with the check.

Count pages before paying: $39.00 covers up to two, each added page or attachment is $8.00, and non-standard formatting adds $20.00. After recording, a certified copy gives you proof, priced at $2.00 per page plus $1.00 for the seal.

faqs.q: How much will recording my Brown County deed cost?
faqs.a: Up to two pages costs $39.00, then $8.00 for each extra page or attachment, and $20.00 more if the paper is non-standard. State law, section 317.32, is the basis.

faqs.q: Where do I mail a deed in Brown County?
faqs.a: Address it to the Brown County Recorder, 800 Mt. Orab Pike, Suite 151, Georgetown, OH 45121, and enclose a cover note with your phone number, a check payable to the recorder, the auditor's fees and forms, and a stamped return envelope.

faqs.q: How is the Brown County conveyance charge figured?
faqs.a: The rate is $4.00 for each $1,000 of price, plus fifty cents per parcel number to the auditor. Questions go to the auditor, 937-378-6398.

faqs.q: Will the recorder's staff write my deed?
faqs.a: No. The office will not draft documents, sell forms or answer legal questions. Have a lawyer or title company prepare it, then get Tax Map and auditor stamps before the recorder.

faqs.q: When does Brown County collect property tax?
faqs.a: Dates shift, so call the treasurer at 937-378-6705. House Bill 186 delayed the latest second-half deadline.
